OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Improving power grid operations is essential for enhancing flexibility and accelerating grid decarbonization. Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise in this domain, most notably through the Learning to Run a Power Network (L2RPN) competition series, but prior work has primarily focused on single-agent settings, neglecting the often decentralized, multi-agent nature of grid control. We fill this gap with MARL2Grid-TR, the first multi-agent RL (MARL) benchmark for grid topology and redispatching, developed in collaboration with transmission system operators. Built on RTE France’s high-fidelity simulation platform, our benchmark supports decentralized control across substations and generators, with configurable agent scopes, observability settings, expert-informed heuristics, and safety-critical constraints. The benchmark includes a suite of realistic scenarios that expose key challenges, such as coordination under partial information, long-horizon objectives, and adherence to hard physical constraints. Empirical results show that current MARL methods struggle under these real-world conditions. By providing a standardized, extensible platform, we aim to advance the development of scalable, cooperative, and safe learning algorithms for power grids.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.17726.title: TSRL: Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Continual Agent Training
arXiv|arxiv:2610.17726.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents excel at complex, multi-step tasks but suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual learning--acquiring new skills often degrades previously mastered capabilities. Existing post-training paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is sample-efficient but prone to severe forgetting, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) preserves prior capabilities but converges slowly without expert guidance. To bridge this gap, we introduce Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning (TSRL), a framework that integrates the strengths of both paradigms through an adaptive, state-dependent expert supervision mechanism. TSRL employs RL as the optimization backbone, activating SFT selectively on "hard states" where the policy fails. Theoretically, we show that restricting supervision to failure states derives an upper bound on the cumulative parameter updates, thereby reducing forgetting compared to full SFT. Empirically, TSRL achieves consistent gains across three agent benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, and Deep Search) at both 7B and 32B scales. In continual learning scenarios, our method retains up to 9.6 points more capability on prior tasks than SFT->RL baselines, while matching or exceeding target-task performance.

We further develop a dual-path evaluation framework that combines Textual Assessment and Visual Assessment. Experiments across nine deep research systems show that TVIR-Agent achieves strong overall performance, underscoring the importance of explicit multimodal design and evaluation for evidence-driven report generation.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.31851.title: Modeling Event-Conditioned Emotional Expression Response with LLM Agents in a Synthetic Social Simulation
arXiv|arxiv:2611.31851.abstract: Emotions are central drivers of human behavior, yet most behavioral models fail to capture their role in shaping perception, decision-making, and collective action. Application areas such as emergency response and public health are especially constrained by the lack of emotion-aware modeling. While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into agent-based models (ABMs), little work has examined how to endow LLM agents with emotional reasoning or validated their ability to reproduce empirically observed emotional patterns. This study addresses this gap by introducing a hierarchical prompting framework that conditions LLM agents with demographic, psychological, and contextual cues to generate event-conditioned emotional responses to real-world events. We validate the resulting event-conditioned emotional responses against large-scale social media reaction data derived from the Social Science One Facebook URL Shares Dataset, complemented by demographic and personality benchmarks. Our simulation results reproduce both polarized and consensus-driven emotional patterns with significant fidelity, supporting the application of LLM agents for emotion-aware modeling in behavioral simulations. We also find, however, that systematic gaps in emotional expression of LLM agents and human populations exist, such as the underexpression of anger relative to human baselines. As such, these findings highlight the need for continued calibration if LLM agents are to serve as proxies for human populations in behavioral modeling. By quantifying their divergence from human populations in terms of emotional expression, we hope that our methods can aid in this effort.
